meta.title: Who really said "There is nothing quite so tragic as a young cynic, because it means the person has gone from knowing nothing to believing nothing"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Real and datable: Maya Angelou said it on camera in Bill Moyers' PBS documentary Facing Evil, 28 March 1988. The "pitiful" version is a later variant.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is nothing quite so tragic as a young cynic, because it means the person has gone from knowing nothing to believing nothing'?
meta.ogDescription: Angelou really said it - PBS's Facing Evil, 28 March 1988, transcript online. The widely reprinted "nothing so pitiful" wording is a later variant.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Angelou said this on camera in Facing Evil, the Bill Moyers PBS documentary broadcast on 28 March 1988, speaking to the symposium on evil the programme filmed in Salado, Texas. The transcript published on billmoyers.com ↗ carries this exact wording, and Quote Investigator ↗ reaches the same conclusion, recommending the 1988 version over the variant that later entered circulation.

source.excerpt: So out of this evil, which was a dire kind of evil, because rape on the body of a young person more often than not introduces cynicism, and there is nothing quite so tragic as a young cynic, because it means the person has gone from knowing nothing to believing nothing.
trail: 28 March 1988 — Angelou speaks the sentence on camera in Facing Evil, the Bill Moyers PBS special produced and directed by David Grubin. Moyers’ own site publishes the transcript of the broadcast ↗, which carries the wording verbatim.

1988 — the symposium volume Facing Evil: Light at the Core of Darkness, edited by Paul Woodruff and Harry A. Wilmer for Open Court (Open Library record ↗), prints an edited transcript of Angelou’s remarks, according to Quote Investigator ↗.
1997 — Simpson’s Contemporary Quotations logs the line under “Maya Angelou poet” with the source line “PBS 28 Mar 88” — but with “tragic” swapped for “pitiful,” as Quote Investigator documents ↗.
Today — Wikiquote ↗ still carries the “pitiful” variant sourced to a 2005 anthology, while Quote Investigator recommends the 1988 spoken version. That is the version quoted at the top of this page.
source.excerptNote: Angelou’s own sentence, as transcribed on billmoyers.com. The famous quotation is the second half of it; the first half is what she is actually talking about.

author.name: Maya Angelou
author.heading: Who said it
author.metaLine: 1928–2014 · American memoirist, poet and civil rights activist
author.bio: Born Marguerite Annie Johnson in 1928, Maya Angelou became one of America’s most widely read memoirists with I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969), which follows her life up to the age of seventeen. She worked as a dancer, singer, screenwriter, director and university professor, and was active in the civil rights movement. Her name is now one of the internet’s favourite hooks for unsourced inspirational lines — which makes the ones that do have a date and a tape worth marking clearly.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — unusually, for a famous Angelou line. What circulates wrongly is the wording, and the source most people reach for.

items.who: “There is nothing so pitiful as a young cynic…”
items.why: A reworded form — “nothing so pitiful as a young cynic because he has gone from knowing nothing to believing nothing” — entered the reference books. Quote Investigator ↗ records it in Simpson’s Contemporary Quotations (1997), notes that “tragic” had been changed to “pitiful,” and recommends using the 1988 spoken version instead.

Wikiquote ↗ lists the “pitiful” variant sourced to The Truth in Words (2005) by Neal Zero — an anthology, not the original. Citing a quote book instead of the broadcast is how a well-documented line still ends up looking unverifiable.

items.who: Unsourced quote cards and image macros
items.why: Shared as a standalone aphorism, the sentence reads like generic uplift. In the actual transcript ↗ it sits inside Angelou’s account of surviving childhood rape, which is what the remark is about.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is genuinely Angelou’s, spoken on camera in Facing Evil, broadcast 28 March 1988 — and the words at the top of this page are what she actually said, per the broadcast transcript ↗.

context.heading: Why she said it
lead: The setting was not a greeting card. Facing Evil was a 1988 PBS documentary built around a Salado, Texas conference on how people live with evil, and Angelou was telling that room about being raped as a child and the years of silence that followed. Reading and learning, she said, were what carried her through — and the line about the young cynic is her account of what she thinks she narrowly escaped.

That is the part the quote-card version loses. Angelou is not making a general remark about kids these days; she is describing a specific fork in the road for someone whose trust has been broken early, and arguing that cynicism only looks like wisdom because it arrives at the same shrug from the opposite direction.
detailsBody: Most viral Angelou lines fail the first test: no book, no speech, no date. This one passes it twice over — the broadcast transcript is online with a date on it, and the compilers noticed early. When Simpson’s Contemporary Quotations picked the line up in 1997, its source line read simply “PBS 28 Mar 88,” as Quote Investigator records ↗.
The one thing that did drift was a single adjective. If you have seen the sentence with “pitiful” where this page has “tragic,” you have seen the reference-book version rather than the spoken one.
